title: 9  Examp prep
text:
13.2 C2. Interpreting an individual’s change

Scenario. For a vertical-jump test: MDC95 = 2.5 cm and SWC = 1.0 cm. An athlete improves from 42.0 cm to 44.0 cm (a +2.0 cm change).
(a) Is this change likely “real” (beyond noise)? (b) Could it be practically meaningful? (c) What does it mean when a change beats the SWC but not the MDC?



Model answer


(a) +2.0 cm is smaller than the MDC95 (2.5 cm) -> you cannot be confident it is a real change rather than measurement noise.
(b) It exceeds the SWC (1.0 cm) -> it is large enough to be practically meaningful if it is real.
(c) Beating SWC but not MDC = the change is practically interesting in size but statistically uncertain -> treat it cautiously, keep monitoring, don’t over-react to one test.

title: 9  Examp prep
text:
13.3 C3. Bland-Altman device comparison

Scenario. A coach considers swapping calibrated force plates for a cheaper jump app. A Bland-Altman analysis (App - Plates) over 40 jumps gives bias = +1.5 cm and 95% limits of agreement = -2.0 cm to +5.0 cm. The SWC for jump height is 1.0 cm.
(a) What does the bias tell you? (b) What do the limits of agreement add? (c) Should the two be used interchangeably for tracking change?



Model answer


(a) Bias +1.5 cm -> the app systematically reads ~1.5 cm higher than the plates on average (a fixed offset).
(b) Limits of agreement (-2.0 to +5.0 cm) -> describe the random error: any individual jump could differ anywhere in that range. The bias alone doesn’t show this.
(c) Not interchangeable for tracking change — the error band (and even the bias) is larger than the SWC (1.0 cm), so device differences would swamp the change you’re trying to detect. Pick one device and stick with it.

title: 9  Examp prep
section: 13.4 C4. Validity + reliability for test selection
text:
13.4 C4. Validity + reliability for test selection

Scenario. Two tests for a basketball squad:

Test 1 (agility): CV = 2.0%; correlates with on-court defensive performance at r = 0.75.
Test 2 (straight sprint): CV = 1.8%; correlates with on-court performance at r = 0.25.

Which would you prioritise for ongoing sport-specific monitoring, and why? What validity issue does the weak sprint correlation highlight?



Model answer


Prioritise Test 1 (agility).
Both are similarly reliable (CV ~2%), so reliability doesn’t separate them.
Validity does: Test 1’s r = 0.75 shows a strong link to actual on-court performance; Test 2’s r = 0.25 is weak.
A reliable-but-not-valid test consistently measures the wrong thing — low monitoring value.
The weak sprint link points to an ecological / criterion validity problem: a straight-line sprint doesn’t reflect the multidirectional demands of the sport.

title: 9  Examp prep
section: 13.5 C5. Why root-2 in the MDC formula
text:
13.5 C5. Why root-2 in the MDC formula

Self-check. In MDC95 = TE x 1.96 x sqrt(2), why is the typical error multiplied by sqrt(2)?



Model answer


A change score is the difference between two measurements (test and retest).
Each measurement carries its own error, so the difference combines two independent errors.
Combining two independent errors makes the variances add, and the SD of the difference scales by sqrt(2) -> hence the term. (The 1.96 sets the 95% confidence level.)

title: 9  Examp prep
text:
13.6 C6. Load-monitoring recommendation

Self-check. A coach wants an in-season monitoring program. Recommend one external and one internal load metric, and explain why using both together beats either alone.



Model answer


External (example): GPS total distance / high-speed running / accelerations — what the athlete did (the work performed).
Internal (example): sRPE or HR-based load / HRV — the athlete’s physiological & perceptual response to that work.
Why both: external = the dose, internal = the response/cost. The same external load can produce very different internal responses depending on fitness, fatigue, heat, sleep, stress.
The relationship between them (e.g., a high internal response to a normal external load) is an early flag for fatigue, illness or maladaptation — which neither metric reveals alone.

If you can confidently separate centre vs spread, read r / r² and a scatterplot, tell apart the reliability (CV, TE) and validity types, classify internal vs external and objective vs subjective load, interpret p-values, the 68-95-99.7 rule and Bland-Altman (bias vs LoA), and reason about SWC vs MDC for individual change — then you’re across the concepts this exam tests. Re-do any item you hesitated on.

The smallest worthwhile change (SWC, often 0.2 x SD) is best described as:

 the smallest change we can detect above measurement noise the smallest change considered practically or meaningfully important the typical error of the test the p-value threshold

The minimal detectable change (MDC) is best described as:

 the smallest change that exceeds measurement error (i.e. a real change, not noise) the smallest change worth caring about practically the bias between two devices the correlation between test and retest

In the formula MDC95 = TE x 1.96 x the square root of 2, the square root of 2 appears because:

 because there are two athletes because the SD is doubled because two measurements (test and retest) each carry error, so the errors combine because you convert the result to a percentage

Case 1 — Is the change real? (meaningful change)
A swimmer’s countermovement jump is measured every Monday. Across a training block the value drifts up and down by a centimetre or two week to week, then rises by 4 cm the week after a taper.

Which of these movements would you treat as noise, and which as a meaningful change?
What would you need to know about the test itself to make that call?

Case 2 — Can we trust the cheaper device? (agreement)
A team trials a low-cost wrist heart-rate sensor against the chest strap they normally trust. The two track closely at rest but diverge during high-intensity efforts.

How would you investigate whether the cheaper unit is good enough to rely on?
What would you plot or summarise to describe how well they agree?
Would you be comfortable swapping between the two to track an athlete’s change over time?
Why is “the two are strongly correlated” not the same as “the two agree”?

Case 3 — Which test earns a place? (reliability + validity for a decision)
A rugby academy wants one test to monitor “match fitness”. Test A is a treadmill run that is highly repeatable between days. Test B is a repeated-sprint protocol that is a little more variable day to day but looks much more like the demands of a match.

What trade-off are you weighing between these two?
What evidence would push you toward one over the other?
Could you justify keeping both? On what grounds?

Case 4 — Filling out the picture (dose and response)
A coach currently records only GPS distance for each session and asks you to build a fuller monitoring picture.

What would you add to capture how the athletes respond to that load, and why?
What are the trade-offs (cost, athlete burden, what it actually tells you) of the tools you would suggest?
How would viewing dose and response together let you spot something neither shows alone?

Case 5 — Same session, different toll (internal vs external load)
Two athletes complete the identical prescribed session — the same external load on GPS — but one reports a much higher session-RPE and shows an elevated heart rate for the same work.

Which measures here are external load, and which are internal?
What might explain the mismatch between them?
What, if anything, would you do with that information the following day?

Case 6 — Significant, but useful? (prediction + hypothesis testing)
A study reports that a fitness-test score is “significantly” related to match high-speed running (p < 0.01, r = 0.30). A coach wants to use the test to predict each player’s match output.

What does the significant p-value tell you here — and what does it not?
Is a correlation of this size strong enough to predict an individual athlete’s output?
What would you advise the coach?

Lit Review feedback






Referencing and academic writing: Common issues included inconsistent reference lists, incorrect citation formatting, use of quotes throughout the review, and citation errors (e.g., first author names, multiple parentheses, full paper titles within text). Recommendation: carefully review referencing guidelines and proofread citation formatting prior to submission.
Historical/contextual development of the tool: Historical sections were often overly generic (e.g., “observation → HR → GPS”) without sufficient detail regarding the evolution of methods, technologies, timelines, or key studies. Recommendation: treat this section as a sourced historical timeline and discuss the development of the specific technology/tool in more depth and context.
Validity and reliability: This was generally the weakest section across many reviews despite representing a major component of the marking criteria. Many students relied on broad statements rather than reporting specific outcomes from primary studies (e.g., CV, TE, ICC, correlation coefficients). Recommendation: anchor claims to specific validation/reliability studies, report actual statistical outcomes, and prioritise deeper interpretation of one or two key papers rather than broad superficial summaries.
Depth over breadth: Stronger reviews tended to demonstrate genuine depth and understanding of a smaller number of studies, rather than superficially discussing many papers. Recommendation: focus on critically analysing a few highly relevant studies and clearly explain what they demonstrate regarding the monitoring tool.
Framework application and conceptual understanding: Many students referenced concepts such as external vs internal load without identifying the originating framework or meaningfully applying it throughout the review. Recommendation: introduce one relevant framework early and consistently return to it to help structure interpretation and discussion.
Balance across sections and marking criteria: Some reviews devoted substantial space to lower-weighted sections (e.g., conclusions/future directions) while providing minimal detail in highly weighted sections such as validity and reliability. Recommendation: align the depth and word allocation of sections with the assessment weighting and marking rubric.
Future directions and practical implications: Future directions were often broad, generic, or disconnected from the evidence discussed throughout the review. In some cases, students shifted toward entirely different technologies/tools in the conclusion. Recommendation: ensure future directions logically emerge from limitations, gaps, or findings identified within the review itself and remain directly related to the chosen monitoring tool.
